raw_findings.message: The operator token is embedded in the source and used as the default credential, so anyone who knows the published value can authorize close and adjust commands when the environment variable is unset.
Wrapping subtraction turns a spent amount above the daily limit into a huge allowance, allowing subsequent transfers to bypass the limit.
Calling split_payment with an empty recipient list divides by zero and panics.
Negative deposit amounts are accepted and debit the account without transfer or daily-limit checks.
A deposit can overflow the signed balance, causing a panic in debug builds or a wrapped, incorrect balance in release builds.
A negative transfer passes the balance check and is queued, so settlement credits the source and debits the destination.
Each queued transfer checks only the current balance and does not reserve pending outflows, so multiple individually affordable requests can settle into an overdraft.
A rejected over-limit transfer resets the spend counter, allowing later transfers to use a fresh daily allowance.
Closing an account only sets a flag; later deposits, transfers, fees, interest, and adjustments still operate on it because those operations do not reject closed accounts.
A negative fee is accepted as a credit and its cast to u64 corrupts the account's daily-spend counter.
An invalid numeric argument makes parse_cents panic, so a malformed command or batch line terminates the process instead of returning an error.
The user-controlled statement filename is joined without validation, allowing paths such as ../../target to write outside the reports directory.
A negative daily limit is cast to u64 and becomes an enormous allowance, effectively disabling the account's spending limit.
A negative account index is cast to usize and then used for indexing, causing a panic when account-at is invoked with a negative value.
Account names are serialized without escaping, so a name containing a newline and forged record can inject or alter ledger records when the state file is next loaded.

raw_findings.message: The operator token is embedded in the source, so anyone who can inspect the binary or source can supply it to authorize `close` and `adjust`.
If spending exceeds the limit, `wrapping_sub` turns the remaining allowance into a huge value and can let subsequent transfers bypass the daily limit.
Calling `split` with an amount but no recipients divides by zero and panics.
Mutating operations do not reject closed accounts, so an account can still receive deposits and initiate transfers after `close` marks it closed.
A negative deposit is accepted as an unrestricted withdrawal, allowing callers to reduce an account balance without transfer or daily-limit checks.
Adding an attacker-supplied deposit to the balance is unchecked, so an overflowing amount can panic in debug builds or wrap and corrupt the balance in release builds.
Negative transfer amounts pass the balance check and skip the daily-limit check, then settlement debits the destination and credits the source.
Settlement debits queued transfers without rechecking available funds, so multiple queued transfers or a later withdrawal can make the source balance negative.
A negative fee credits the account while casting the negative amount to `u64` increases its spending counter by a huge value.
Malformed or out-of-range monetary input reaches `unwrap` and panics instead of being rejected as a command error.
The user-controlled statement filename is joined without validation, so a name such as `../../target` can make the command overwrite files outside the reports directory.
A negative limit is cast to `u64`, producing an enormous daily allowance that effectively disables the intended limit.
The user-supplied account index is used without bounds checking, so a negative or out-of-range index panics the process.
Account names are written raw into the line-oriented state format, so a name containing a newline and crafted record can inject account records when the state is loaded again.

raw_findings.message: The operator token is embedded in the source and is used as the default when no environment override is set, so anyone who can run the program can authorize `close` and `adjust` using this known value.
Interest is calculated with `f64`, which loses cent-level precision for sufficiently large balances and can produce an incorrect credited amount.
When spent exceeds the limit, `wrapping_sub` returns a very large allowance, allowing subsequent transfers to bypass the daily limit.
Integer division drops any remainder, so a split such as 10 cents among 3 recipients accounts for only 9 cents.
Calling `split` with an amount but no recipients divides by zero and panics.
Opening an already-used name creates an ambiguous duplicate, while lookups and operations silently select only the first matching account.
Operations do not reject accounts marked closed, so a caller can continue depositing to or transferring from an account after it is closed.
A negative deposit is accepted as a debit, letting callers withdraw funds through `deposit` without the transfer checks or daily-limit accounting.
Balance mutations use unchecked signed arithmetic, so sufficiently large deposits, fees, interest, adjustments, or settlements can panic or wrap and corrupt balances.
Negative transfer amounts pass the balance check and are queued, causing settlement to credit the source and debit the destination.
Each queued transfer checks only the current balance and does not reserve earlier pending debits, so multiple individually affordable requests can settle into an overdraft.

An over-limit request resets the spent counter before returning an error, and the caller persists that error-state mutation, allowing the caller to regain daily allowance by making a rejected request.
A negative fee credits the account while casting the negative amount to `u64` adds a huge value to the daily-spending counter.
Malformed or out-of-range numeric command arguments make `parse_cents` panic instead of returning a handled input error.
Every account statement includes the ledger-wide audit history, exposing other accounts' names and transaction details to anyone able to request a statement.
The output name is joined without restricting traversal or absolute paths, so `statement --out` can overwrite files outside the reports directory.
Casting a negative signed limit to `u64` turns it into a huge positive limit, allowing an account to bypass its intended daily cap.
A negative index is cast to a huge `usize`, and any out-of-range index then panics when `account_at` indexes the account vector.
An invalid persisted balance is silently replaced with zero, so a malformed state file can erase an account's balance without reporting a load error.
Account names are written into the line-oriented format without escaping, so a name containing a newline and crafted record text can inject accounts or other records when the state is reloaded.
